paper_title: RPDR: A Round-trip Prediction-Based Data Augmentation Framework for Long-Tail Question Answering
summary:
RPDR: A Round-trip Prediction-Based Data Augmentation Framework for Long-Tail Question Answering - Yiming Zhang, Siyue Zhang, Junbo Zhao, Chen Zhao, 2025

RPDR targets the failure mode of dense retrievers in long-tail open-domain QA, where rare entities are poorly represented and BM25 often outperforms embedding-based retrieval on low-frequency questions. The task setting is single-fact QA over Wikidata-derived subject relation object triples, evaluated on PopQA and EntityQuestions with test partitions stratified by entity frequency, including an extreme long-tail split with entity frequencies between 10 and 100. The framework has three stages. First, it synthesizes long-tail QA pairs from unpopular Wikipedia backed Wikidata triples, filtering by subject-page popularity below 1e6 monthly views and retaining only examples whose answer string appears in the top 1000 BM25-retrieved passages; this yields about 86k augmentation samples for PopQA and 126k for EntityQuestions. Second, it trains an inverse embedding model following text embedding inversion to reconstruct text from a dense retriever embedding. Third, it scores each synthetic question by round-trip recoverability, using S(x) = 1 minus the normalized L2 distance between the original embedding and the embedding of the reconstructed text, and keeps only high-score examples as easy-to-learn augmentation data for contrastive fine-tuning of Contriever.

The main empirical claim is that dense retrieval can be made competitive on long-tail QA if augmentation data are selected by reversibility rather than sampled indiscriminately. On PopQA long-tail retrieval, RPDR reaches R@10 74.5 versus 55.0 for NV-Embed and 66.8 for the same augmentation pool sampled randomly, a 19.5 point gain over the strongest embedding baseline and a 7.7 point gain over RPDR-random. On EntityQuestions long-tail retrieval, RPDR reaches R@10 54.6. In end-to-end RAG, retrieval gains transfer to exact-match QA accuracy: with GPT-3.5 as generator, RPDR improves long-tail EM on PopQA from 29.7 with Contriever to 41.4, an 11.7 point increase; the paper also reports up to 10.9 percent improvement on long-tail queries overall when paired with an LLM reader. Ablations show that training on unrecoverable synthetic samples degrades performance, supporting the claim that round-trip filtering suppresses harmful long-tail augmentation and mitigates forgetting. Manual error analysis further localizes RPDR’s advantage to syntactically simple but semantically rare entities such as disambiguation-sensitive names, while performance remains weak on orthographically complex entities; based on this, the authors train a routing classifier over 10k augmented samples to switch between RPDR and BM25, improving PopQA long-tail R@10 from 74.5 to 79.1 and EntityQuestions long-tail R@10 from 54.6 to 58.4, with a reported 4.6 percent gain over RPDR alone on PopQA.
